1071	\subsection{The integer type of a range}
1072	\seclabel{revival-ranges}
1073	
1074	\begin{description}
1075	\item[Affected sections] \secref{ranges}; \secref{basic-integers};
1076	\secref{revival-numbers}; \secref{revival-notrevised}.
1077	\item[Change] The components of an explicit range are values of type
1078	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, into which an integer numeral converts, and it is a static
1079	error if a component has another integer type. A paragraph shows how a loop
1080	whose counter must have a wider integer type is written: over a range of
1081	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} values, widening each element.
1082	The box in \secref{basic-integers}, the effect of \secref{revival-numbers} and
1083	\secref{revival-notrevised} no longer say that a range over two different
1084	integer types infers the narrowest type that both coerce into; they keep that
1085	rule for a generic call.
1086	\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival decided
1087	it on 27~September 2026.
1088	The Working Draft named no integer type for a range, and \library\ declared
1089	their ranges generic over an integer type named by a type parameter. The
1090	compiled type checker refused that code wherever it converted a numeral to the
1091	range's integer type, since a numeral does not convert to a type named by a
1092	type parameter (\secref{using-coercion}).
1093	The compiled path's own smaller library declares its ranges over
1094	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} alone (\nolinkurl{Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi}, lines
1095	173--174), and on the Java Virtual Machine, which runs Fortress, an array holds
1096	at most $2^{31}-1$ elements, so a range of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} values indexes any
1097	of them.
1098	With every range over \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, no range is over two different
1099	integer types, and the rule that infers the narrowest type that both coerce
1100	into concerns a generic call alone.
1101	The full reasoning is in
1102	\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-ranges/decision-record.md}
1103	in the revival's repository.
1104	\item[Effect] A program writes a range over \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} where it wrote
1105	one over \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}64} or
1106	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, and widens its elements where it needs a wider counter; a
1107	range over another integer type is refused. Whether a \KWD{nat} parameter may
1108	be a component of a range is not settled (\secref{revival-notrevised}).
1109	\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/ranges.tex},
1110	lines 42--44:
1111	\begin{quote}
1112	An \emph{explicit range}
1113	is self-contained and completely describes a set of integers.  Assume that
1114	$a$, $b$, and $c$ are expressions that produce integer values.
1115	\end{quote}
1116	The box in \secref{basic-integers} and two sentences of this appendix are the
1117	revival's own text of 27~September 2026, not the Working Draft's.
1118	The box said, in \nolinkurl{Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex}, lines
1119	61--65, before this revision:
1120	\begin{quote}
1121	A generic call or a range over two different integer types is to infer the
1122	narrowest type that both coerce into, by a rule to be written into
1123	\chapref{type-inference} together with its implementation; until then such a
1124	call writes its static argument, as in
1125	\EXP{f\llbracket\mathbb{Z}64\rrbracket(a, b)}.
1126	\end{quote}
1127	The effect of \secref{revival-numbers} said:
1128	\begin{quote}
1129	A generic call or a range over two different integer types writes its static
1130	argument until the rule that infers the narrowest type both coerce into is
1131	written into \chapref{type-inference} together with its implementation.
1132	\end{quote}
1133	and \secref{revival-notrevised} said:
1134	\begin{quote}
1135	The rule by which a generic call or a range over two different integer types
1136	infers the narrowest type that both coerce into is to be written into
1137	\chapref{type-inference} together with its implementation
1138	(\secref{revival-numbers}).
1139	\end{quote}
1140	\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
1141	\end{description}
1142	
1143	\subsection{Examples and a property with ranges over wider integer types}
1144	\seclabel{revival-range-examples}
1145	
1146	\begin{description}
1147	\item[Affected sections] \secref{block-expr}; \secref{defining-generators},
1148	\figref{generatorDefn} and the generator adapted to a commutative monoid;
1149	\secref{basic-integers}.
1150	\item[Change] The function \VAR{mySum} of \secref{block-expr} takes a parameter
1151	of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and keeps its sum of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}.
1152	The generator of \figref{generatorDefn}, and the generator of
1153	\secref{defining-generators} that adapts it to a commutative monoid, are
1154	declared over \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and the figure's midpoint is
1155	\EXP{\VAR{lo} + (\VAR{hi} - \VAR{lo}) \div 2}.
1156	The factorial property of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} is stated by the value at \EXP{0} and
1157	a recurrence, without a range.
1158	\item[Rationale] Each built a range over an integer type other than
1159	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} (\secref{revival-ranges}): the loop of \VAR{mySum} over
1160	\EXP{0\COLONOP{}i} with \VAR{i} of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, the method
1161	\VAR{seq} of the figure's generator over \EXP{\VAR{lo}\COLONOP\VAR{hi}} with
1162	bounds of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, and the property's product over
1163	\EXP{1\COLONOP{}m} with \VAR{m} of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}. The adapted generator
1164	builds no range in its own text, but its ellipsis stands for the figure's
1165	members.
1166	The figure's midpoint \EXP{\left\lfloor (\VAR{lo}+\VAR{hi})/2 \right\rfloor} is a
1167	value of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} (\secref{basic-rationals}), which converts to
1168	neither \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} nor \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} (\secref{basic-integers}), so
1169	the recursive construction of the generator did not accept it; the new
1170	midpoint is a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} value equal to it whenever \EXP{\VAR{lo} \leq \VAR{hi}}
1171	and the generator's size \EXP{\VAR{hi}-\VAR{lo}+1} is a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} value, and
1172	it does not form the sum \EXP{\VAR{lo}+\VAR{hi}}, which exceeds \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}
1173	when both bounds are large.
1174	The property of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} holds for every natural \VAR{m}; over a range
1175	of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} values it would hold only below $2^{31}$ and need two
1176	conversions, so it is stated by a recurrence, as \secref{basic-integers} states
1177	the binomial coefficient by Pascal's rule.
1178	\item[Effect] None beyond the examples and the property.
1179	\item[Original text] The two examples are typeset from the files
1180	\nolinkurl{SpecData/examples/basic/Expr.Do.mySum.fss} and
1181	\nolinkurl{SpecData/examples/advanced/Generators.GeneratorDefn.fss} of the
1182	revival's repository, identical in the commit of 2~February 2011 of which
1183	\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/} is a copy and unchanged until this
1184	revision;
1185	\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/blocks.tex}, line 72,
1186	and \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced/parallelism-locality/defining-generators.tex},
1187	line 50, input them. As typeset from those files:
1188	\begin{quote}
1189	\begin{FortressCode}
1190	\VAR{mySum}(i\COLON\mathbb{Z}64)\COLON\mathbb{Z}64 =\; \KWD{do} \\
1191	\2\+\VAR{acc}\COLON\mathbb{Z}64 \ASSIGN 0 \\
1192	  \KWD{for} j \leftarrow 0\COLONOP{}i \KWD{do} \\
1193	  \2\+\VAR{acc} \ASSIGN \VAR{acc} + j\- \\
1194	  \KWD{end} \\
1195	  \VAR{acc}\- \\
1196	\KWD{end}
1197	\end{FortressCode}
1198	\end{quote}
1199	and
1200	\begin{quote}
1201	\begin{FortressCode}
1202	\KWD{object} \TYP{BlockedRange}(\VAR{lo}\COLON \mathbb{Z}64, \VAR{hi}\COLON \mathbb{Z}64, b\COLON \mathbb{Z}64) \KWD{extends} \TYP{Generator}\llbracket\mathbb{Z}64\rrbracket \\
1203	\2\+\VAR{size} \COLONOP \mathbb{Z}64 = \VAR{hi} - \VAR{lo} + 1 \\
1204	  \VAR{seq}(\KWDVAR{self})\COLON \TYP{SequentialGenerator}\llbracket\mathbb{Z}64\rrbracket = \VAR{seq}(\VAR{lo}\COLONOP\VAR{hi}) \\
1205	  \VAR{generate}\llbracket{}R\rrbracket\bigl(\VAR{reduction}\COLON \TYP{Reduction}\llbracket{}R\rrbracket, \VAR{body}\COLON \mathbb{Z}64\rightarrow{}R\bigr)\COLON R = \\
1206	  \2\+\KWD{if} \VAR{size} \leq (b \OPR{MAX} 1) \KWD{then} \\
1207	    \2\+\fortressonelinecomment{(*}{ Blocks smaller than b run sequentially }{*)} \\
1208	      r \COLONOP R \ASSIGN \VAR{reduction}.\VAR{empty}(\ultrathin) \\
1209	      i \COLONOP \mathbb{Z}64 \ASSIGN \VAR{lo} \\
1210	      \KWD{while} i \leq \VAR{hi} \KWD{do} \\
1211	      \2\+v \COLONOP R = \VAR{body}(i) \\
1212	        r \ASSIGN \VAR{reduction}.\VAR{join}(r,v) \\
1213	        i \mathrel{\mathrel{+}=} 1\- \\
1214	      \KWD{end} \\
1215	      r\- \\
1216	    \KWD{else} \\
1217	    \2\+\fortressonelinecomment{(*}{ Blocks larger than b are split in half and generated in parallel. }{*)} \\
1218	      \VAR{mid} = \left\lfloor\,{\textstyle\VAR{lo}+\VAR{hi}\over\textstyle2}\,\right\rfloor \\
1219	      \VAR{reduction}.\VAR{join}(\+\TYP{BlockedRange}(\VAR{lo},\VAR{mid},b).\VAR{generate}\llbracket{}R\rrbracket(\VAR{reduction},\VAR{body}), \\
1220	                     \TYP{BlockedRange}(\VAR{mid}+1,\VAR{hi},b).\VAR{generate}\llbracket{}R\rrbracket(\VAR{reduction},\VAR{body}))\-\- \\
1221	    \KWD{end}\-\- \\
1222	\KWD{end} \\
1223	 \\
1224	f(\ultrathin) = \bigl\langle\,2\, x \bigm| x \leftarrow \TYP{BlockedRange}(1,10,3)\,\bigr\rangle
1225	\end{FortressCode}
1226	\end{quote}
1227	\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced/parallelism-locality/defining-generators.tex},
1228	lines 405, 407 and 411, the three lines of the adapted generator that named
1229	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, quoted without their indentation and alignment commands:
1230	\begin{quote}
1231	\begin{Fortress}
1232	\( \KWD{value}\;\;\KWD{object} \TYP{BlockedRange}(\VAR{lo}\COLON \mathbb{Z}64, \VAR{hi}\COLON \mathbb{Z}64, b\COLON \mathbb{Z}64) \KWD{extends} \TYP{Generator}\llbracket\mathbb{Z}64\rrbracket\)\\
1233	\(   \VAR{generate}\llbracket{}R \KWD{extends} \TYP{CommutativeMonoid}\llbracket\,R, \oplus\rrbracket, \KWD{opr} \mathord{\oplus}\rrbracket(\VAR{body} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}64 \rightarrow R) \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} R = \;\KWD{do}\)\\
1234	\(         i \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}64 = l\)\\
1235	\end{Fortress}
1236	\end{quote}
1237	\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex}, lines 559--561:
1238	\begin{quote}
1239	\begin{Fortress}
1240	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{property} \forall (m)\; m! = \prod\limits_{k\leftarrow{}1\COLONOP{}m} k\)\-\\\poptabs
1241	\end{Fortress}
1242	\end{quote}
1243	\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
1244	\end{description}
1245	
1246	\subsection{Passages not yet revised}
1247	\seclabel{revival-notrevised}
1248	
1249	No passage that instantiation exclusion or the reorganized numeric types
1250	contradict is known to be unrevised.
1251	The rule by which a generic call over two different integer types
1252	infers the narrowest type that both coerce into is to be written into
1253	\chapref{type-inference} together with its implementation
1254	(\secref{revival-numbers}). The result of an integer raised to a negative power is not yet given (\secref{basic-integers}; \secref{revival-integers}).
1255	Whether a \KWD{nat} parameter, which may appear wherever a variable of type
1256	\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} can (\secref{natparams}), may be a component of a range
1257	is not settled (\secref{revival-ranges}); the static ranges of
1258	\secref{ranges} and the examples whose ranges a \KWD{nat} parameter bounds are
1259	not revised.
1260	Before the number chapters were revised, this section said:
1261	\begin{quote}
1262	The number chapters, \chapref{lib:numbers-basic} (whose integers are \secref{basic-integers})
1263	and \chapref{lib:numbers-advanced}, are not yet revised.
1264	Their nested tower, in which each integer type is a subtype of the rational
1265	one above it and each carries its algebra at its own type, and the
1266	conditional self-extension of \TYP{RationalQuantity}, are refused by
1267	instantiation exclusion, as the compiled type checker refuses the
1268	library's nested tower today.
1269	They will be revised together with the reorganization of the library's
1270	numeric types that route~A decides, and not before, because a
1271	specification ahead of its library is as much an open discrepancy as one
1272	behind it.
1273	Until then the rule refuses the tower these chapters describe.
1274	\end{quote}
1275	
1276	\subsection{Route C, the alternative not taken}
1277	\seclabel{revival-routec}
1278	
1279	The team's 2012 patent applications (US~8,843,887 and US~8,898,632;
1280	Chase, Steele, Naden, Hilburn, and Luchangco) relax the rule for a
1281	self-typed parameterized trait: a type may be a subtype of several of its
1282	instantiations when they form a chain.
1283	The revival built that rule whole as an experiment and measured it.
1284	It closes the unsoundness that instantiation exclusion guards against only
1285	together with a rule on return types over every level of a chain and a
1286	change in how a call chooses among generic methods specialised to
1287	different instantiations: 188 lines of code in five files of the compiled
1288	type checker and code generator.
1289	Reversing route~A for route~C would also need a method per level of a
1290	chain in the code generator, work in the interpreter, a way past a stack
1291	overflow of the type checker on the self-typing clauses, and seven library
1292	declarations, besides undoing the reorganization of the library's numeric
1293	types.
1294	Route~C rescues none of the \KWD{where}-clause examples of
1295	\secref{where-clauses} nor the \TYP{Nothing} of \secref{convenience-types},
1296	each of which places one type below infinitely many instantiations, which
1297	no chain contains.
1298	Under route~C the numeric chapters could have kept the nesting of their
1299	widths, and their original text, quoted in \secref{revival-numbers} and the
1300	entries after it and kept in the Working Draft of February 2011, is route~C's
1301	for that nesting; route~C rescues neither the refined number types nor
1302	\TYP{RationalQuantity} (\secref{revival-numbers}).
1303	The record of the experiment is
1304	\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/mie-probes/route-c-experiment.md} in the
1305	revival's repository.
1306	\fussy

250	whose parameters must be \emph{instantiated} 
251	with \emph{static arguments} 
252	to produce a trait type.
253	The resulting type is an \emph{instantiation} 
254	% (with the arguments) 
255	of the generic type.
256	% Victor: Does this sentence belong here?  (Perhaps only in traits chapter.)
257	The trait or object declaration may impose conditions on the arguments 
258	with which its static parameters may be instantiated.
259	% Victor: I had "with which the generic type may be instantiated"
260	%   which does not technically follow the terminology established above,
261	%   though I don't think anyone would be confused.
262	See \chapref{traits} for more of static parameters 
263	and how they may be instantiated.
264	
265	For convenience, 
266	we consider a trait or object declaration without static parameters
267	to define a generic type (with no parameters)
268	whose unique instantiation 
269	is the trait type defined by the declaration.
270	Thus, 
271	properties of instantiations of generic types 
272	also apply to trait types defined by 
273	non-parameterized trait and object declarations.
274	
275	% Victor: I just made up this terminology.
276	%  Is there standard terminology, or better alternatives?
277	We say that one generic type $G$ 
278	\emph{determines} another generic type $G'$ 
279	if every parameter of $G'$ is a parameter of $G$.
280	Given an instantiation $I$ of $G$, 
281	the \emph{corresponding instantiation} of $G'$ 
282	is the one in which the parameters of $G'$ are instantiated 
283	with the corresponding arguments of $I$.
284	
285	% If a non-generic trait or object declaration has an \KWD{extends} clause, 
286	% then the trait type it defines 
287	% is a subtype of every type listed in the \KWD{extends} clause.
288	% If it has an \KWD{excludes} clause
289	% then the trait type it defines 
290	% excludes every type listed in the \KWD{excludes} clause.
291	% If it has a \KWD{comprises} clause 
292	% then the trait type it defines is covered by 
293	% the union of the types listed in the \KWD{comprises} clause.
294	
295	Every trait type is a subtype of \Object\ and \Any, 
296	and a supertype of \Bottom.
297	A trait or object declaration may have an \KWD{extends} clause, 
298	which specifies a set of types and 
299	generic types determined by the generic type defined by the declaration.
300	% Victor: Do we have a term for this set?
301	%   Perhaps it should be defined in the traits chapter.
302	An instantiation of the generic type defined by such a declaration 
303	is a subtype of every type in this set, 
304	and of the corresponding instantiation of each generic type in this set.
305	
306	% Victor: Suppose we define the "extends set" for every trait or object declaration
307	%   (it is empty if there is no extends clause).  Then we could write:
308	% An instantiation of a generic type defined by a trait or object declaration 
309	% is a subtype of every type in the extends set of that declaration
310	% and of the corresponding instantiation of each generic type
311	% in the extends set of the declaration.
312	
313	% A trait or object declaration may have an \KWD{extends} clause, 
314	% which specifies a set of types and generic types.
315	% Every parameter of any generic type in this set
316	% must be a static parameter of the trait or object declaration.
317	% An instantiation of the generic type defined by such a declaration 
318	% is a subtype of every type in this set, 
319	% and of the instantiation of each generic type in this set 
320	% in which the parameters are instantiated with corresponding arguments.
321	
322	A static parameter of a trait declaration 
323	may be declared with the \KWD{covariant} modifier.
324	In this case, 
325	% the generic type defined by the trait declaration 
326	% is \emph{covariant} in that parameter.
327	% Victor: I had the above text,
328	% but it was convenient to define "covariant parameter":
329	it is a \emph{covariant parameter} 
330	of the generic type defined by the trait declaration.
331	% Victor: the following sentence is a bit unwieldy.
332	One instantiation of a generic type 
333	is a subtype of another instantiation of the same generic type 
334	if the argument instantiating each covariant parameter 
335	in the first instantiation 
336	is a subtype of the corresponding argument 
337	in the second instantiation, 
338	and the argument instantiating each non-covariant parameter 
339	is the same in both instantiations.
340	
341	Every trait type excludes \Void, \Bottom\ and every tuple type.
342	Every trait type other than \Object\ 
343	also excludes every arrow type and function type.
344	A trait declaration may have an \KWD{excludes} clause, 
345	which also specifies a set of types and 
346	generic types determined by the generic type defined by the declaration.
347	% Victor: Do we have a term for this set?
348	%   Perhaps it should be defined in the traits chapter.
349	An instantiation of the generic type defined by such a declaration 
350	excludes every type in this set 
351	and the corresponding instantiation of each generic type in this set.
352	
353	% Multiple instantiation exclusion
354	% Victor: I've shortened this to instantiation exclusion.
355	Fortress also imposes a rule called \emph{instantiation exclusion}:
356	% which defines the exclusion relation for different instantiations of a generic type:
357	Two instantiations of a generic trait type exclude each other 
358	if the corresponding arguments for any covariant parameter exclude each other, 
359	or if the corresponding arguments for any non-covariant parameter 
360	are not type equivalent.
361	\note{I believe this exactly characterizes exclusion
362	among different instantiations of a generic type, 
363	but the rule we impose is stronger:
364	Any trait that extends (possibly indirectly) 
365	two instantiations of a generic type 
366	must extend an \emph{expressible} instantiation of that generic type 
367	that is a subtype of both.
368	In other words,
369	among all instantiations of a generic type 
370	that are supertypes of some expressible trait type, 
371	one must be a subtype of all the others, 
372	and it must be expressible.
373	This section should say only which instantiations exclude each other,
374	as it does.
375	It perhaps should make it clearer that what is said here 
376	is a consequence of instantiation exclusion, 
377	which is a rule applied to trait declarations.}
378	
379	
380	% An object trait type is a leaf type:
381	An object trait type has no strict subtype other than \Bottom, 
382	and it excludes any type that is not its supertype.
383	
384	A trait declaration may have a \KWD{comprises} clause, 
385	which also specifies a set of types and 
386	generic types determined by the generic type of the declaration.
387	An instantiation of the generic type defined by such a declaration 
388	is covered by the union 
389	of the types in this set 
390	and the corresponding instantiations of the generic type in this set.
391	
392	% Victor: I'm not sure about the proper terminology here.
393	A trait or object declaration may provide a \emph{coercion} from a type or a generic type.
394	(See \secref{coercion-decl} and \chapref{coercion}.)
395	If a trait or object declaration provides a coercion from a type, 
396	then any instantiation of the generic type defined by that declaration 
397	coerces that type.
398	If it provides a coercion from a generic type, 
399	then an instantiation of the generic type defined by that declaration 
400	coerces the corresponding instantiation of the generic type of the coercion.

568	\section{Intersection and Union Types}
569	\seclabel{internal-types}
570	
571	For every finite set of types, there is a type denoting a unique
572	\emph{intersection} of those types.
573	The intersection of a set of types $S$ is a subtype of every type $T \in S$
574	and of the intersection of every subset of $S$.
575	There is also a type denoting a unique \emph{union}
576	of those types. The union of a set of types $S$ is a supertype of every
577	type $T \in S$ and of the union of every subset of $S$.
578	Neither intersection types nor union types are first-class types;
579	they are used solely for type inference (as described in
580	  \chapref{type-inference}) and
581	they cannot be expressed directly in programs.
582	
583	The intersection of a set of types $S$ is equal to a named type $U$ when
584	any subtype of every type $T \in S$ and of the intersection of every
585	subset of $S$ is a subtype of $U$.
586	Similarly, the union of a set of types $S$ is equal to a named type $U$ when
587	any supertype of every type $T \in S$ and of the union of every
588	subset of $S$ is a supertype of $U$.
589	For example:
590	%trait S comprises {U,V} end
591	%trait T comprises {V,W} end
592	%trait U extends S excludes W end
593	%trait V extends {S,T} end
594	%trait W extends T end
595	\begin{Fortress}
596	\(\KWD{trait} S \KWD{comprises} \{U,V\} \KWD{end}\)\\
597	\(\KWD{trait} T \KWD{comprises} \{V,W\} \KWD{end}\)\\
598	\(\KWD{trait} U \KWD{extends} S \KWD{excludes} W \KWD{end}\)\\
599	\(\KWD{trait} V \KWD{extends} \{S,T\} \KWD{end}\)\\
600	\(\KWD{trait} W \KWD{extends} T \KWD{end}\)
601	\end{Fortress}
602	because of the \KWD{comprises} clauses of $S$ and $T$ and the \KWD{excludes}
603	clause of $U$, any subtype of both $S$ and $T$ must be a subtype of
604	$V$.  Thus, $V = S \inter T$.
605	
606	
607	Intersection types (denoted by $\inter$) possess the following properties:
608	\begin{itemize}
609	\item Commutativity: $T \inter U = U \inter T$.
610	\item Associativity: $S \inter (T \inter U) = (S \inter T) \inter U$.
611	\item Subsumption: If $S \Ovrsubtype T$ then $S \inter T = S$.
612	\item Preservation of shared subtypes: If $T \Ovrsubtype S$ and $T \Ovrsubtype U$ then $T \Ovrsubtype S \inter U$.
613	\item Preservation of supertype: If $S \Ovrsubtype T$ then $\forall U.~S \inter U \Ovrsubtype T$.
614	\item Distribution over union types: $S \inter (T \uni U) =
615	  (S \inter T) \uni (S \inter U)$.

371	definitions using \emph{abstract function declarations}.
372	Abstract function declarations themselves may be overloaded.
373	For an abstract function declaration with name \VAR{f}, argument type
374	\VAR{T}, and return type \VAR{U} (\VAR{T} and \VAR{U} may be tuple types),
375	any concrete declaration for \VAR{f} must be for a function whose argument
376	type is a subtype of \VAR{T} and whose return type is a subtype of \VAR{U}.
377	Furthermore, the union of the argument types of the concrete declarations for
378	\VAR{f} must be equal to \VAR{T}.
379	Concrete function declarations must satisfy the overloading rules.
380	Unless \VAR{T} has a \KWD{comprises} clause (or is a tuple type, at least
381	one of whose entries has a \KWD{comprises} clause), this implies that some
382	concrete declaration for \VAR{f} must have argument type \VAR{T}.

385	without a body.  Parameter names may be elided but parameter types cannot

# Decision record: the specification's ranges over ZZ32 (rung U, climb batch 7R)

This is the decision record the S1 form asks for (`explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`, 2026-09-26, S1): each revised passage, the original, the new text, why it changed, and the way back. Appendix I's entry "The integer type of a range" (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:1071-1141`) names this file. The base is `26c5d3dd7`. "The Working Draft of February 2011" is the unrevised copy under `Specification-1.0-frozen/` (POSITIONS 2026-09-26, the first of the batch-5 answers). In `ranges.tex`, `blocks.tex` and `defining-generators.tex` the base's lines equal the frozen copy's (`diff`, no output), so each line cited below in those files is also the frozen copy's line; `basic-integers.tex` and `changes.tex` were revised by the revival before this rung, and their base lines are given as base lines.

The decision this rung carries out is the ranges decision (POSITIONS 2026-09-27, the numerics plans, the synthesis's decision 1, "Option 1, ZZ32"): the one library's scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only; the specification's ranges section, its two `ZZ64` examples, `ZZ`'s factorial property and the revival's callout at `Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:61-65` are revised in the S1 form; a range over another integer type becomes a static error; a wider counter is written as a `ZZ32` loop that widens its index. Rung J builds the library beside this rung and is not in this rung's tree; section 6 lists every statement the revised text makes that the gather checks against J's landed library.

## 1. The list

The list, written before any edit and committed first (`cb4551e2d`), is `probes/list.txt`: eight passages revised (R1 to R8), twelve left (L1 to L12), and one defect measured on the way (M1). Measurement C's scanner, re-run on this worktree, gives the same sixteen candidate lines as measurement C (`probes/list/nonzz32-rerun.txt`, `probes/list/nonzz32-local.py`, which differs from `explorations/reviews/numerics-plan-coordinator/probes-C/nonzz32.py` in its root only). The list adds four finds to measurement C's section 3:

- R7, the Effect of Appendix I's "The number types" (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:479-481` at the base), a third repetition of the callout's range half;
- R8, a second `BlockedRange` over `ZZ64` typeset inline in the same section as the figure (`Specification/advanced/parallelism-locality/defining-generators.tex:382-427` at the base, `:389-434` now), which builds no range in its own lines and so escaped the scanner;
- L3, ranges bounded by a `nat` static parameter (`SpecData/examples/basic/Fun.Decl.fss:23`; `Specification/advanced-lib/binary.tex:716-717`, `:951`, `:1086-1089`; `Specification/basic/matrix-unpasting.tex:160-161`), which the decision does not settle;
- M1, the original `Generators.GeneratorDefn` failing under walk on the base before it builds any range.

## 2. What the revision states, and what it does not

The ranges section states:
- the components of an explicit range are values of type `ZZ32`; `a`, `b` and `c` produce such values (the `#` operand `n` is a component too);
- an integer numeral converts to `ZZ32`, as the literals section says libraries define coercions from numerals to integers (`Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:146-148`);
- it is a static error if a component has an integer type other than `ZZ32`;
- a loop whose counter must have a wider integer type runs over a range of `ZZ32` values and widens each element, shown as `for i <- 0#n do j: ZZ64 = i ... end`, where the binding converts by the coercion the integer chapter states (`Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:25`: `ZZ64` coerces from `ZZ32` and `NN32`).

It does not state: the public range traits' index type, which the decision keeps generic and the section never named; multi-dimensional ranges, which the section never described; the type of `|r|`; anything about static ranges (L2) or `nat` parameters as components (L3). Each is left as the Working Draft had it, so the revised text states no more than J's section builds (the batch record's stop).

## 3. Per passage: the original, the new text, the reason, route C

Each original is quoted in Appendix I, in the entry named.

### 3.1 The ranges section (R1; Appendix I, "The integer type of a range")

- Original, `Specification/basic/expressions/ranges.tex:42-44` (frozen `:42-44`): "An explicit range is self-contained and completely describes a set of integers. Assume that a, b, and c are expressions that produce integer values."
- New text, `ranges.tex:42-48`: "Its components are values of type ℤ32: assume that a, b, and c are expressions that produce such values. An integer numeral converts to ℤ32 (§ literals), and it is a static error if a component of an explicit range has an integer type other than ℤ32." And `:78-91`, after the three bullets: "A loop whose counter must have a wider integer type runs over a range of ℤ32 values and widens each element, as in the following loop, where the binding converts i to ℤ64 (§ basic-integers)", with the loop typeset by `Fortify/fortify.el` from its `%` source (`probes/build/fortify-output.txt`). The callout follows at `:92-99`.
- Reason: the decision. The bounds are ZZ32 because the one library's operators become `opr :(lo:ZZ32, hi:ZZ32)` and `opr #(lo:ZZ32, ex:ZZ32)` (J), as the compiled path's own library already declares them (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi:173-174`, and `trait Range extends GeneratorZZ32` at `:143`); a size is an `NN32` value and a JVM array's length at most 2^31-1 (POSITIONS 2026-09-27, a size's range). The later restart's ranges section is a heading only (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/Expressions/ranges.tick:12`), so there is nothing to cite beside (POSITIONS 2026-09-26, the lineage note).
- The bullets (`:50-76` now, `:46-72` at the base) are unchanged: they define each range arithmetically, and with ZZ32 components they hold as written (L1).

### 3.2 The callout and its two repetitions (R5, R6, R7; Appendix I, "The integer type of a range")

- The revival's own text of 27 September 2026 (`d9c415395`), not the Working Draft's, so Appendix I quotes it from the base with its base path and lines, as the brief asks.
- `Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:61` at the base: "A generic call or a range over two different integer types is to infer the narrowest type ..."; the Effect of "The number types", `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:479` at the base: "A generic call or a range over two different integer types writes its static argument until ..."; "Passages not yet revised", `changes.tex:1076` at the base: "The rule by which a generic call or a range over two different integer types infers ...".

L1 to L12 of `probes/list.txt`. The ones that go to Pavol or to the ledger:

The rung takes none: the passages are left, and one sentence of "Passages not yet revised" (`changes.tex:1255-1259`) says the question is open. It goes to Pavol.
- **L9**, the adapted generator's midpoint: a slip of the Working Draft, left and reported.
- **L10**, Appendix I's introduction: reported for the gather.

1. **The ranges section says "its components are values of type ℤ32"**, not "a, b, c and n": the bullets use `n` both as a derived count (`ranges.tex:51`, `:59` now) and as the operand of `#` (`:68`), and the section's own word for the operands is "components" (`:101-103` now, "Non-static components of a range expression"). Rejected: adding `n` to "Assume that a, b, and c", which would collide with the count.
2. **The wider counter is shown with a typed binding, `j: ZZ64 = i`**, not with the library's `widen(i)` that the decision's wording and the demos use (`ProjectFortress/demos/fact64.fss:22-23`): the specification states the coercion into ℤ64 (`basic-integers.tex:25`) and names no integer `widen`; walk converts at a typed binding (FACTS.md, "Under walk, the interpreter converts by coercion at its three kinds of type check"), measured on the base: the loop sums to 3 and the binding holds a `ZZ64` (`RespelledRanges-base-walk.txt`, W1, W2). Rejected: `widen(i)`, a library method the specification does not list. It is placed after the bullets that define `#`, with the callout after it.
3. **`mySum` changes its parameter only.** Rejected: all of it ZZ32, which changes the sum's type and loses what a ZZ64 sum is for (S2); keeping `i: ZZ64` and narrowing it (`0:narrow(i)`), a library method the specification does not list and a function that fails for a large `i`.
4. **The generator is respelled over ZZ32 throughout, with `mid = lo + (hi - lo) DIV 2`.** Rejected: keeping ZZ64 fields and producing a `SequentialGenerator[\ZZ64\]` from a ZZ32 range by a map, which teaches conversions instead of blocked ranges; keeping the floor midpoint, which is a ℤ (section 3.4); `(lo + hi) DIV 2`, which truncates toward zero (`basic-integers.tex:431-432`), so for `BlockedRange(-3,-2,1)` it gives `hi` (`(-3 + -2) DIV 2` is `-2` under walk, `RespelledRanges-base-walk.txt`, G5) and the first half is the whole range again, recursing without end, and which forms `lo + hi`, past ZZ32 when both bounds exceed 2^30 (row 453's shape in the compiler library). The new midpoint equals the floor whenever `lo <= hi` and the generator's size `hi - lo + 1` is a ZZ32 value; at `(-1, 2147483647)` it raises `IntegerOverflow` at `hi - lo` on both paths (`probes/skeptic/differential3.txt:2-31`), where the generator's own `size` overflows first. The team's sequential loop, `i += 1` after the last element, is kept; at `hi = MAX` it raises `IntegerOverflow` after the last body, row 451's shape, not this rung's.

Its midpoint is left (L9).

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""reanchor.py BASE [--apply] : re-anchor the citations of lines of the chapters this rung edits,
in the assert messages and comments of ProjectFortress/tests/, compiler_tests/ and library_tests/,
by the map of unchanged lines from `git show BASE:<chapter>` to the working tree (difflib's equal
blocks). J's four restated files are skipped (the gather re-anchors them). A citation is
'<chapter>.tex:N', ':N-M' or 'N,' and every following ', :K' continuation that belongs to it.
Each cited line is mapped; a line inside a changed block is reported and left. Prints one line per
citation: file:line, old -> new, and whether the text at the new line equals the text at the old."""
import difflib, re, subprocess, sys, glob, os
BASE = sys.argv[1]; APPLY = '--apply' in sys.argv
CHAPTERS = {'ranges': 'Specification/basic/expressions/ranges.tex',
            'basic-integers': 'Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex',
            'defining-generators': 'Specification/advanced/parallelism-locality/defining-generators.tex',
            'blocks': 'Specification/basic/expressions/blocks.tex',
            'changes': 'Specification/appendices/changes.tex'}
SKIP = {'ProjectFortress/tests/RangePrototype.fss', 'ProjectFortress/tests/XXXRangeBoundsRungO.fss',
        'ProjectFortress/tests/XXXSeqRangeTopRungO.fss', 'ProjectFortress/tests/XXXRangeSizeZZ64RungO.fss'}
maps, old_text, new_text = {}, {}, {}
for short, path in CHAPTERS.items():
    old = subprocess.run(['git', 'show', f'{BASE}:{path}'], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.split('\n')
    new = open(path).read().split('\n')
    m = {}
    for tag, i1, i2, j1, j2 in difflib.SequenceMatcher(None, old, new, autojunk=False).get_opcodes():
        if tag == 'equal':
            for k in range(i2 - i1): m[i1 + k + 1] = j1 + k + 1
    maps[short], old_text[short], new_text[short] = m, old, new
CIT = re.compile(r'(?P<ch>ranges|basic-integers|defining-generators|blocks|changes)\.tex:(?P<rest>\d+(?:-\d+)?(?:, ?:?\d+(?:-\d+)?)*)')
def mapnum(ch, n, where):
    if n not in maps[ch]:
        print(f'  UNMAPPED {where} {ch}:{n} (inside a changed block)'); return None
    return maps[ch][n]
files = [f for d in ('ProjectFortress/tests', 'ProjectFortress/compiler_tests', 'ProjectFortress/library_tests')
         for f in sorted(glob.glob(d + '/*.fss'))]
changed = 0
for f in files:
    if f in SKIP: continue
    src = open(f).read(); lines = src.split('\n'); out = []
    for ln, line in enumerate(lines, 1):
        def repl(mo):
            global changed
            ch = mo.group('ch'); rest = mo.group('rest')
            def one(tok):
                a = tok.split('-'); nums = [int(x) for x in a]
                new = [mapnum(ch, x, f'{f}:{ln}') for x in nums]
                if None in new: return tok
                ok = all(old_text[ch][x - 1] == new_text[ch][y - 1] for x, y in zip(range(nums[0], nums[-1] + 1),
                         range(new[0], new[0] + nums[-1] - nums[0] + 1)))
                res = '-'.join(str(x) for x in new)
                print(f'{f}:{ln}: {ch}:{tok} -> {ch}:{res}  text {"equal" if ok else "DIFFERS"}')
                return res
            parts = re.split(r'(, ?:?)', rest)
            newrest = ''.join(p if i % 2 else one(p) for i, p in enumerate(parts))
            if newrest != rest: changed += 1
            return f'{ch}.tex:{newrest}'
        out.append(CIT.sub(repl, line))
    if APPLY and out != lines:
        open(f, 'w').write('\n'.join(out))
print(f'# {changed} citation groups changed' + (' (applied)' if APPLY else ' (dry run)'))

## 2. The ways, weighed

The library's own practice first (POSITIONS 2026-09-19; 2026-09-24, after the diagonal). The units: library lines; rungs, each with its gated test; the count stage's reading (22 on the tree, 87 once the api's checks run, `RangeInternals` 21 unchanged; ways note section 2); the interpreter tests (422) and the two microGPT checks (40 of 40).

### The library's own way: the open marker (way 1)

- What. `trait AnyIntegral extends { Number } end`, as the team wrote the markers above its other generics, `AnyMaybe`, `HasRank` and `AnyList`, each open, with `excludes` and a "not yet: comprises X[\T\] where [\T\]" comment (`.fsi:882-885`, `:1129-1130`; `Library/List.fsi:52-56`). The api stood so from 2009 to `02d09a39f` (2026-09-19).
- Clears. The checker error; count 87 (ways note way 1; rung H section 6).
- Walk. Refuses the library at load: the generic scalar block's `MAX[\T extends Number, I\]` against `StandardTotalOrder[\T\].MAX` has no excluding pair (`rung-exclusion-remainder/probes/integral/open-MicroGptFlatCheck.txt:8-14`). The clause was added for exactly this (`02d09a39f`'s message, POSITIONS 2026-09-21).
- How the library gets round the blocking rule. Maessen's own advice, "add excludes { Number }" (`82c85b03a`), cannot apply: a number is an order and a group, so the exclusion would be false. The placeholder device (`AnyAdditiveGroup`'s pattern, `.fsi:255-260`) applied to the orders gets walk past `MAX` and stops it at `+` against `AdditiveGroup.+`; arrays cannot exclude `AnyAdditiveGroup`, since `Vector` and `Matrix` are additive groups (ways note way 1). The block written per element type is 56 declarations; walk was not run on it.
- Cost. Two library lines, blocked at walk; ten more for the placeholders, still blocked. The placeholders clear 8 of the api's 66 whatever else is done (79 on the count), which is batch 7b's rung L's material, not this decision's.
- Verdict. The library's way is blocked by the library's own generic scalar block, which Pavol approved as landed (POSITIONS 2026-09-21).

### The team's compiled-world way: the self-type idiom, `comprises I` (way 3)

- What. `trait Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\] ... comprises I`, `AnyIntegral`'s clause kept. Ryu's idiom of 2009 (`3a8ad3b67`), the compiler library's (`Library/CompilerAlgebra.fsi:16`, `:24`, `Equality[\T\] comprises T`, `StandardTotalOrder[\T\] ... comprises T`), and Naden's reading (section 1, item 4). The checker's rule was designed to accept it (section 1, item 7).
- Clears. The checker error with no checker change; count 87; one message then prints the self type `(Integral[\I\] & {I})` (ways note way 3).
- Walk. Overflows its stack at load (row 407; `probes/integral/self-MicroGptFlatCheck.txt:22-60`). A 6-line edit in `BuildEnvironments.finishTrait` stops it, by leaving a type variable out of a trait's recorded clause; with it C4's check loads and 38 check lines are identical within the 600-second cut (ways note way 3, `captures/walk/c4-self-w407.txt`). The full checks and the 422 interpreter tests were not run.
- Specification. A type variable is not "a declared trait identifier" (`traits.tex:161-165`). The Types chapter does not forbid it; Welterweight's grammar has no place for it (section 1, items 5 and 6). The S1 change would legalise a form the group's 2012 calculus dropped.
- Forecloses and risks. It is the library's first self type. Route A was chosen against route C, whose device is `comprises T` on the self-typed traits, and route C's experiment overflowed the checker's `Formula` with it on eight traits (POSITIONS 2026-09-24, route A; FACTS, "Route C built whole as a shadow"; `reviews/exclusion-design-brief.md:59`, `:128`). With one trait the count stage finishes. Nothing in the record says what the distance does under it. By reading it could clear `Integral`'s share of the distance's class S1, "a generic trait's `self` is not its parameter", 28 errors such as `floor(self):I = self` (`perf-probes/prelude/distance-triage.md:99`; `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:652`); the class also holds the orders' bodies (`:279`, `:332`), which the one-trait form does not reach and the eight-trait form overflows. Unmeasured, so a gap (section 4), not a credit.
- Cost. Two library lines; one interpreter rung of about 6 Java lines with its gated test (an original-tree edit, test first); one specification rung; the interpreter tests, both microGPT checks and the distance to measure in the gate.

### The library-only redesign: `Integral` leaves the number tower (way 2, `skexcl`)

- What. `Integral[\I\]` without `AnyIntegral` in its `extends` clause (the keep-the-rule sketch, `reviews/mie-probes/keep/flat-tower-sketch.fsi:77-79`), plus the exclusions it had through `Number` restated by hand: `excludes { AnyMaybe, AnyUniqueItem, HasRank }`. The five keep `AnyIntegral`.
- Clears. The checker error; count 87. Walk loads, and both microGPT checks pass 40 of 40, every check line identical (ways note way 2, `captures/walk/skexcl-*.txt`). The interpreter tests and the distance were not run.
- Specification. Met under every reading, since `AnyIntegral`'s immediate subtypes become exactly the five; the number chapters still hold (ways note way 2). No specification change.
- Forecloses. `Integral[\I\]` is no longer a `Number`: a body over `I extends Integral[\I\]` loses `Number`'s members, today `asFloat` and `=` (`.fsi:281-289`), unless it bounds `I` by `Number` too. The generic traits that exclude `Number` (`Generator[\E\]`, `Array1`, the strided factories' trait, `Array3`) cannot be named in `Integral`'s clause without a `where` clause, so `Integral` stops excluding them; whether walk's overload check needs any of those pairs is what the interpreter tests would show. The hand-written list must follow `Number`'s from then on.
- Against the record. It rewrites the team's hierarchy against their own comment on the line, which closes `AnyIntegral` to `Integral`'s instantiations (`.fsi:434`). It is a fix designed round the checker's rule, which the decision of 2026-09-19 rules out ("No fix is designed from a reading of the specification alone or from a user-side workaround").
- Cost. Two or three library lines per file, one library rung; the cheapest in lines, the largest in design.

### The parked accommodation, narrow form (way 11)

- What. A third disjunct in `isEligibleToExtend` (`TypeHierarchyChecker.scala:254-266`): a generic immediate subtrait of a closed trait is eligible when at least one trait in the checker's table extends it and every such trait is below a listed type (`everyKnownSubtypeListed`, 14 lines, `perf-probes/nat/zero.md:59-63`; `anyintegral-comprises-ways/shadow-thc.py:46-64`). The condition `!tt.getArgs.isEmpty` restricts it to a generic subtrait, the one kind the later Types chapter says cannot be listed.
- Clears. The checker error; count 87, the `FortressLibrary` row 132, the same error list as every clearing way (ways note way 11, `captures/count/narrow-base.txt`). It refuses the false list `zElig.fss` (`B[\X\] extends S` with nothing below `B`) and accepts `zElig2.fss`, whose list is true (`captures/probes/switches.txt`; `perf-probes/nat/zero/zElig.fss`, `zElig2.fss`). The two expected failures that pin the ellipsis rule, `XXX3q` and `XXX10p`, fail as pinned, and none of the 39 compiler tests with a clause changes (ways note way 11). The broad form (way 10, 5 lines) accepts `zElig` and turns the team's `Compiled9.z` from 2 errors to 1; it is not recommended.

- On record. Approved and parked on 2026-09-21, "the flattening making it moot" (POSITIONS 2026-09-21, the library commit; `PLAN.md`, item 21 and the parked line); climb batch 7's rung H measured that the flat library does not make it moot (`rung-exclusion-remainder/REPORT.md` section 6).

### The rest, blocked by measurement or by the record

- Way 4, the team's 2008 clause on `Integral[\I\]` with the instance rule: 124 on the count (37 new errors on each integer type's own operators against `Integral`'s), two team tests changed (`XXX10h`, `XXX10n`), walk 40 of 40. It is the only way that refuses a program's own integral type. The Types paper and Welterweight require a listed type to be below the trait at its own parameters, which `ZZ` is not for every `I` (ways note way 4). Not recommended: the highest cost, against the group's 2011 and 2012 texts.
- Way 5, `Number`'s clause carrying the closure: the error moves up a level, or walk refuses the library as in way 1 (ways note way 5). Batch N's rung Q edits `Number`'s clause for `IntLiteral`, which extends `Number`, not `AnyIntegral` (`coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-N.md:255`, `:276`); it does not touch this question.
- Way 6, the generic named bare: refused before the hierarchy check, "Type requires static arguments" (ways note way 6).
- Way 7, api and component differing: refused by the specification (`Specification/basic/components/source-code.tex:372-381`) and the export checker (ways note way 7).
- Way 8, the ellipsis: refused by the checker for every api-declared extender (row 354) and by the specification's note (`traits.tex:241-246`) (rung H section 6).
- Way 9, the team's `where` spelling: no grammar for it (`traits.tex:88`), unimplemented on both paths (row 331), and the Types chapter does not let `AnyIntegral` list a generic it does not determine (ways note way 9).

### Leave it (way 12)

- The count stage stays at 22 and never runs the api's overloading and return-type checks; the distance stage counts the 66 already (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-7/gate/distance.txt:1-12`).
- The manifests of batch 7R and batch N were written expecting the api's rows on the count stage "since batch 7's H" (`coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-7R.md:124`, `:219`; `CLIMB-BATCH-N.md:609`), which is not so on the tree; both stages are reported and never red, so no gate goes red for it. ## 4. What the record does not hold

Named as gaps, not probed (protocol principle 5).

- The distance stage under any clearing way. The ways note's runs were stopped on the coordinator's narrowing (its section 5); by reading, the change is the two H2 errors. The rung's gate measures it.
- Way 3's interpreter tests, its full microGPT checks and its distance, so whether `Integral`'s share of the S1 class (28) clears under `comprises I` on one trait. If it does, batch 8 gains a measured way for that share; the recommendation stands, since the orders' share needs the eight-trait form that overflowed.
- Way 2's interpreter tests and distance, so whether any walk overload pairs `Integral[\I\]` against a generic that excludes `Number`.
- Walk on the per-type scalar block (way 1's third form).

The judgement is conditional on none of these: way 11 cannot change a walk output, and its count-stage effect is measured. A deciding fact that could reverse it would be a walk output changed by the clause as written; the tree's own captures say there is none (ways note section 6).

## For Pavol

**Question.** How do we resolve the checker's refusal of `AnyIntegral`'s `comprises` clause, the last early error in the `FortressLibrary` api?

**Context.**

- Refresher. `trait T comprises { A, B }` closes `T`: `A` and `B` are the only types directly under it. The design has it so two traits can be told apart without a `where` clause: closed families that share no member exclude each other, which lets an operator be overloaded on both.
- The shape. `AnyIntegral` is the marker "some integer type" and lists the five integer types. `Integral[\I\]`, the generic interface each integer type implements at itself, sits between them, unlisted. The checker wants every direct child listed; `Integral` cannot be, being generic, and the team's `where` spelling (their "not yet" comment on the line) is unimplemented.
- What the designers said. The 2008 text and the checker's 2009 rule: a child must be listed. The group's 2012 texts (Luchangco's Types chapter, Welterweight): a clause says where a trait's values come from, and a trait in between adds none. Under your decisions of 09-23 and 09-26 the 2012 texts weigh more, and by them the clause is right as written.
- The library's own way, an open marker with `excludes`, is blocked: a number cannot exclude the algebra traits, so walk refuses the generic scalar block.
- Walk passes today: both microGPT checks 40 of 40 with the clause as it stands.

**Options.**

1. Teach the checker the 2012 reading: a generic child of a closed trait is accepted when every type the checker sees under it is listed. 14 Scala lines, gated tests, no team test changes, one S1 specification callout. Walk untouched. The count stage rises 22 to 87 as the api's 66 overloading errors become visible. Approved and parked by you on 09-21.
2. The compiler library's idiom, `Integral[\I\] comprises I`. Passes the checker as is; walk overflows (row 407), so a 6-line interpreter edit, its interpreter tests not yet run; a specification callout legalising a type variable in a clause, which the 2012 calculus dropped; the library's first self type under route A.
3. Take `Integral` out from under `AnyIntegral`, its exclusions restated by hand. Two or three library lines per file; both microGPT checks pass; interpreter tests not run. `Integral` stops being a `Number`, against the team's comment.
4. Leave it. The api's 66 stay off the count stage; it must be resolved before the switch-over anyway.

**A yes to 1** commits you to one small batch of two rungs between 7R and N (checker, specification), a checker rule of ours, reversible by deleting 14 lines, and a ledger row for a hole every option but the 2008 clause shares: a program's own integer type in another file is not caught.

**A no** leaves 7b's overload rung without the count stage's measure of the api and defers the same choice to the switch-over.

**Recommendation.** Option 1: the checker learns the 2012 reading; the clause and walk stay as they are.

find_ant(){

  export NODOTPATH="`echo "$PATH" | sed -e '1,$s/^[.]://g'`"
  NODOTPATH="`echo "$NODOTPATH" | sed -e '1,$s/:[.]:/:/g'`"
  NODOTPATH="`echo "$NODOTPATH" | sed -e '1,$s/:[.]$//g'`"
  result="`(PATH="$NODOTPATH" which ant 2>/dev/null)`"
  if [ -z "$result" ]; then
    echo "Could not find ant. You need to install it. See http://ant.apache.org/ for details." >&2

  fi
  echo $result
  exit 0
}

fi

if [ -z "$JAVACMD" ] ; then

The list of rung X (climb batch 7C), written before any edit, on the base 715816bdd.

Criterion (the batch record, section 3, X, "What it writes"): every passage of Specification/ outside
library/apis/ that says what a comprises clause may list or what it asks of the traits that extend a
closed trait, with what the decision makes of it, whether it is revised now or left, and the source
that settles it. Found from probes/list/grep-comprises.txt (git grep over the base's tracked .tex
files for comprise, immediate sub, immediately extend and ComprisingType, 106 hits), each hit read
with ten lines either side. "The decision" is POSITIONS.md 2026-09-28, AnyIntegral's comprises clause,
"Option 1."; its content for the specification is the judgement's section 3, "The specification
change, in the S1 form" (explorations/reviews/anyintegral-comprises-judgement.md:98-107).

REVISED

R1  Specification/basic/traits.tex:234-246, the draft note. First sentence (:236-240): the types
    listed "are exactly the traits that immediately extend T and they must explicitly extend T".
    Second sentence (:241-246): the ellipsis rule.
    The decision: the first sentence becomes rendered normative text in the later Types chapter's
    reading (Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick:384-390, :277-283; Welterweight,
    Papers/Welterweight/grammar.tick:21-22), with a \revision callout; the ellipsis sentence stays as
    it is, in its note. Revised now. Source: the decision; the judgement, section 3.
    Its Appendix I entry: a new subsection of Specification/appendices/changes.tex immediately
    before "Passages not yet revised" (:1246 on the base), after rung U's two entries.

LEFT, SETTLED BY THE DECISION OR BY R1 ITSELF

L1  traits.tex:156-165. The clauses are sets of trait references; in an API a comprises clause may
    include "..."; "A trait reference listed in the comprises clause is a declared trait identifier
    (within the same component or an API imported by the component)". Left: R1's text says a listed
    type may be an instantiation of a parameterized trait, which a declared trait identifier with
    static arguments is; whether a bare type variable may be listed is not this rung's (the batch
    record, section 3, X, "The decisions": "Not this rung's: ... a type variable in a clause";
    row 407 rests its home on this sentence and the note below it).
L2  traits.tex:166-170, Victor Luchangco's draft note: "do we really mean 'trait identifier' ...?
    Does it include instantiations of parametric traits?" Left as the team's note; answered by R1's
    text (judgement section 3: "Victor's question at :166-170 is answered by the first sentence"),
    and R1's callout says so.
L3  traits.tex:264-297, the Molecule example: ExclusiveMolecule, which extends the closed Molecule
    unlisted, is "not allowed"; OrganicMolecule and InorganicMolecule; InclusiveMolecule (an
    exclusion example). Left: the decision keeps it as it is (judgement section 3, "The Molecule
    example stays as it is"). Under R1 ExclusiveMolecule is still refused: it has no static
    parameters, is a subtype of no listed type and has no comprises clause.
L4  Specification/basic/expressions/var-ref.tex:63-70, the type of self in a trait with a comprises
    clause is T intersected with the union of the traits the clause mentions. Left: it follows from
    R1's first sentence (every value of T is a value of a listed type), and a trait between T and
    its listed types adds no value.
L5  Specification/basic/components/source-code.tex:372-392, an API's clause with "..." is satisfied
    by a component clause listing the API's types and others the component declares. Left: the
    ellipsis rule is not this rung's (row 354; the judgement section 3, "The ellipsis sentence of the
    note (:241-246) is unchanged").
L6  Specification/basic/components/apis.tex:46-60 and Specification/appendices/grammars/
    concrete-syntax.tex:469-493, the grammar of a clause: TraitType lists, "..." in an API, and in
    the appendix's grammar ComprisingType ::= TraitType | Id. Left: R1 adds no syntax; the Id
    alternative is where a naked type variable parses, which is not this rung's (as L1).
L7  Clauses declared in the library chapters: Specification/basic/exceptions.tex:61-67, :115-123 and
    Specification/basic-lib/exception.tex:32-37 (Exception comprises CheckedException,
    UncheckedException); Specification/basic-lib/convenience.tex:38-47 (Maybe[\T\] comprises
    { Nothing[\T\], Just[\T\] }, instantiations at Maybe's own parameter, as R1 allows);
    Specification/advanced-lib/comparison.tex:32-49, :139-154; the "comprises { ... }" of
    Specification/basic-lib/booleans.tex:37, :99, :374, :429 and Specification/advanced-lib/
    binary.tex:102, :150, :421, :432, :591, :614, :795, :861. Left: each lists types that extend
    the trait; none has an unlisted extender.
L8  Specification/appendices/changes.tex:247-278, the revival's entry "The empty optional value",
    which quotes the Working Draft's Maybe[\T\] comprises { Nothing, Just[\T\] }. Left: a quoted
    original.

LEFT AND REPORTED: NEITHER THE DECISION NOR Y'S SECTION SETTLES THE NEW TEXT (the batch record's
stop "A passage of the list whose new text neither the decision nor Y's section settles: the rung
reports it and does not choose")

P1  Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:583-604, section "Intersection and Union Types": with
    trait S comprises {U,V}, trait T comprises {V,W}, U excludes W, "because of the comprises clauses
    of S and T and the excludes clause of U, any subtype of both S and T must be a subtype of V. Thus,
    V = S intersected with T", under the type-level definition of :583-585. The passage reads the
    clauses at the type level. Under R1 a program may add a parameterized trait G[\X\] extending S
    and T, unlisted, whose extenders are all below V; every value of G[\ZZ32\] is a V, but
    G[\ZZ32\] is a subtype of S and T and not of V. The example's own program has no such trait and
    its conclusion holds for it; whether the general reasoning is restated at the value level, or a
    trait that sits between two closed traits is refused, the decision does not say.
P2  Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:275-307, the same example: "Thus, V = S intersected with
    T, and the declaration f(V) 'disambiguates' f(S) and f(T), i.e., it is applicable to and more
    specific for any call to which both f(S) and f(T) are applicable". With P1's G, a call f(g) for
    g : G[\ZZ32\] has f(S) and f(T) applicable and f(V) not applicable by its static type. Same
    question as P1, with the overloading rules' guarantee at stake.
P3  Specification/basic/functions.tex:370-415, abstract function declarations: "the union of the
    argument types of the concrete declarations for f must be equal to T"; with Molecule, "the
    programmer must provide a definition for every immediate subtype of Molecule, or it is a static
    error". Molecule's immediate subtypes are its listed types, so the example holds; for a closed
    trait with a parameterized immediate subtrait between it and its listed types (AnyIntegral with
    Integral), "every immediate subtype" and "every listed type" differ, and the decision does not
    say which the rule means.
P4  Specification/basic/components/source-code.tex:428-434, a team draft note (item 2): a trait with a
    comprises clause "is considered to have a concrete method declaration ... provided that all its
    immediate subtraits are considered to have concrete method declaration with that signature".
    The same question as P3, in a note of proposals.

NOT IN THE CRITERION (grep hits read and set aside)

N1  traits.tex:18-19, a team note pointing to an email "Problem with covariant List?" (no rule).
N2  traits.tex:45, :88, :136, :152, :256, the grammar and the clause order (no rule on what is listed).
N3  traits.tex:208-221, the definition of "immediately extends" and Victor's notes on it. After R1 the
    note that used the term no longer does; the definition is left.
N4  Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:134-136 and Specification/basic-lib/objects.tex:21-22,
    the immediate subtypes of Any ("comprises" as an English verb; Any has no clause).
N5  Specification/appendices/future.tex:269-285, a future-work item: "Identifying the intersection of
    any two types with comprises clauses with the union of their common subtypes ... We agreed to
    revise the Meet rule to address this with the coverage check." The team's own pointer to the
    coverage reading and to P1 and P2's question; not normative.
N6  Specification/appendices/calculi/basic/syntax.tex:78 (Basic Core Fortress omits comprises
    clauses); Specification/basic/components/intro.tex:29 (an api comprising components, another
    construct); Specification/basic/lexical-structure.tex:640, :715, :1205, :1219 and
    Specification/appendices/FAQ.tex:23-24 (the English verb, a heading with no text).

\subsection{The traits that extend a closed trait}
\seclabel{revival-comprises}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{trait-decls}.
\item[Change] The first sentence of a draft note in \secref{trait-decls},
which said that the traits listed in a \KWD{comprises} clause are exactly
the traits that immediately extend the declared trait and that they must
explicitly extend it, is replaced by normative text: every listed type
extends the declared trait \VAR{T}, and every value of type \VAR{T} is a
value of one of the listed types; a listed type may be an instantiation of
a parameterized trait whose static arguments contain no static parameter
other than those of \VAR{T}; and a trait or object that explicitly extends
\VAR{T} is a subtype of a listed type, or a trait with a \KWD{comprises}
clause of its own each of whose listed types meets the same requirement, or
a trait with static parameters that at least one trait or object extends
and every trait or object extending it is a subtype of a listed type.
The note's second sentence, on a clause that includes ``\EXP{\ldots}'', is
kept in its note, and the example of \TYP{Molecule} is unchanged.
The new text answers Victor Luchangco's draft note on trait identifiers
earlier in the section: an instantiation of a parameterized trait may be
listed.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival
decided it on 28~September 2026.
The team's later Types chapter (Luchangco, 2012) reads a \KWD{comprises}
clause as coverage: the clause ``specifies a set of types and generic types
determined by the generic type of the declaration'', and an instantiation of
the declared generic type ``is covered by the union of the types in this set
and the corresponding instantiations of the generic type in this set'', one
generic type determining another ``if every parameter of'' the other ``is a
parameter of'' it
(\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick}, lines
277--283 and 384--390, in the revival's repository).
Welterweight Fortress, the calculus of the type group's paper of 2012
(Chase, Hilburn, Luchangco, Naden, Ryu, Steele, and Tristan, ``Dynamic
Dispatch and Type Inference Semipredicates''), reads it at the level of
values: ``no value can belong to the trait unless it also belongs to one of
the comprised types''; its rule for a trait declaration asks nothing of the
traits that extend a trait with such a clause
(\nolinkurl{Papers/Welterweight/grammar.tick}, lines 21--22;
\nolinkurl{Papers/Welterweight/fig-wellformeddecls.tick}, lines 38--62).
The draft note restated the rule of the compiled type checker of 2009,
under which \library\ could not close their marker of the integer types as
the team meant to: \TYP{AnyIntegral} lists the five integer types, and the
parameterized trait \EXP{\TYP{Integral}\llbracket{}I\rrbracket}, which each
of them extends at itself, stands between them unlisted, as the team's
comment on the declaration records (``not yet: comprises
\EXP{\TYP{Integral}\llbracket{}I\rrbracket} where
\EXP{\llbracket{}I\rrbracket}'', \nolinkurl{Library/FortressLibrary.fsi},
line 434).
\TYP{Integral} has a static parameter that \TYP{AnyIntegral} does not have,
so it cannot be listed, and every value of it is a value of one of the five.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-comprises/decision-record.md}
in the revival's repository.
\item[Effect] The compiled type checker accepts \library's
\TYP{AnyIntegral} as written (\nolinkurl{Library/FortressLibrary.fsi},
lines 433--436).
No example of this specification changes: \TYP{ExclusiveMolecule}, which
has no static parameters, is still not allowed.
The compiled type checker enforces the requirement on a trait with static
parameters over the declarations it sees: a trait or object declared in
another component, below such a trait and a subtype of no listed type, is
not refused (row~487 of the revival's gap ledger).
The interpreter does not check \KWD{comprises} clauses.
The passages that read a \KWD{comprises} clause at the level of types, the
intersection of two traits with such clauses (\secref{internal-types},
\secref{more-specific-rule}) and the definitions an abstract function
declaration requires (\secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations}), are not
revised; whether they are to be restated at the level of values is not
settled.
\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/traits.tex},
lines 230--241, a draft note:
\begin{quote}
If a trait declaration of \VAR{T} includes a \KWD{comprises} clause
then the traits listed in its \KWD{comprises} clause
are exactly the traits that immediately extend \VAR{T}
and they must explicitly extend \VAR{T}
(i.e., list \VAR{T} in their \KWD{extends} clause).
If the \KWD{comprises} clause of a trait \VAR{T} includes ``\EXP{\ldots}''
(and must therefore be in an API),
then in a component exporting the enclosing API,
other traits may explicitly extend \VAR{T},
but these traits may not be declared or imported by the API
(see \secref{apis}).
\end{quote}
Its second sentence is kept, in its note.
\item[Route C] The same under route~C, under which the self-typed traits
carry \KWD{comprises} clauses of their own (\secref{revival-routec}): a
parameterized trait between a closed trait and its listed types then meets
the requirement through its own clause, and the last case of the
requirement is not needed.
\end{description}
